source.title: Gibbs-Based Information Criteria and the Over-Parameterized Regime
source.authors: Haobo Chen; Greg Wornell; Yuheng Bu

record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps model dimension and measures test MSE, testing the size-wise double-descent pattern in a new random-feature setting.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 also plots training MSE, but the text does not separately describe its outcome. The paper's results on BIC and marginal likelihood are not rows for these versions because they do not measure the named test-risk behaviour.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 (left) sweeps the parameter count p of a random-feature model sampled with MALA from a Gibbs posterior (n=200). The authors state that test loss peaks at p=n and then declines below under-parameterized levels. This is the study's own measurement of model-wise double descent in a non-deep model class. It is secondary to the paper's information-criteria aim, but it bears directly on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but it should add the following. Classical AIC/BIC fail to track the double-descent trend of test MSE. The proposed Gibbs-based BICs select the large over-parameterized model. AIC (generalization error) exhibits double descent while BIC (marginal likelihood) does not, and this mismatch is strongly affected by the prior parameter λ.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a model-size sweep and test MSE, but in a two-layer random-feature network with a fixed random first layer; the study also analyzes Gibbs-based information criteria.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the mismatch between KL divergence and generalization error changes with prior parameter λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Gibbs-based BIC (marginal likelihood) favours large p but shows no double descent, unlike population risk. Meanwhile the AIC+ generalization term (symmetrized KL information) and the ℓ2-norm term do show double-descent shapes, and the mismatch depends on the prior λ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Marginal likelihood does not track the double-descent shape of population risk in over-parameterized random-feature models, and the mismatch depends on the prior.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The main double-descent evidence is described in text but its plotted MSE values are not numerically provided. The reported sweep is for one random-feature model setting; error-bar type is not stated.

untested.parts: No deep or conventionally trained networks; only a random-feature model with a fixed first layer.
No test error over training epochs.
No sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold.
Only one model class (random-feature regression) at one n/d/noise setting; no sweep across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
Population risk is plotted for several λ values (Fig. 2 right), but the text does not describe whether the peak shrinks or vanishes. Noise is not varied, and no multiple peaks are reported.
Complexity is not re-counted to test whether the curve becomes U-shaped.

missing.what: Population risk vs p at several prior strengths λ. This could show whether regularization strength removes or shrinks the peak, but the text gives no description of the outcome.
The generalization error term ISKL (AIC+ penalty) vs p at several λ, which the text says shows double-descent behaviour for a given λ.
missing.locator: Section 5, 'Similarity between KL divergence and generalization'; Figure 3 (right)

record.verdict_notes: The double-descent curve is a motivating demonstration in a paper about information criteria. It is evidenced only by a figure plus one sentence, with no numbers. The random-feature setting resembles the RFF experiments in the Belkin et al. original, so the result is close to a replication of V4 in that model class rather than a new class. Verdicts rest on the text's description of Figure 1 (left).

versions.untested_parts: The sweep is in a two-layer random-feature network with a fixed random first layer, not a broad set of conventionally trained deep networks.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The paper does not report test error while varying sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The evidence is for the random-feature model studied, not a sweep across multiple model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The paper does not test whether noise drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
The paper does not test whether re-counting complexity converts the curve into an ordinary U shape.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.size_stated: p varies; interpolation threshold at p = n = 200
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter dimension p and measured test MSE.

conditions.value: two-layer RF model; first-layer weights fixed random, second-layer parameter trained

rows.value: figure only; text states the test-loss peak is at p = n = 200 and test error declines as p increases further
rows.uncertainty: Error bars are reported for experimental settings; type not stated
rows.note: The text identifies the interpolation-threshold peak and subsequent decline, including a decline below the under-parameterized regime.
rows.check: The subject is a two-layer random-feature model with a fixed random first layer and only the second layer trained, i.e. a linear model on random features, not a deep network. The row should therefore not link to V1, which names deep networks. Conditions also omit three things: weights are sampled with MALA from a Gaussian-prior Gibbs posterior (a ridge-like λ penalty), the likelihood noise is fixed at σ=0.05, and the λ used for Figure 1 is not stated. Error bars come from 50 runs (Appendix I.2).

relationships.condition: Random-feature regression, n=200, d=400, σ²=0.1, Gibbs/MALA sampling
relationships.reason: Per the text, test MSE peaks at p=n=200 and then falls below under-parameterized levels as p grows (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE peaked at p=n=200 and then fell below underparameterized levels as p increased.
